lessons.title: Scripts and where they live
lessons.summary: The three kinds of script, where each one runs, and how to set up your practice baseplate.

sections.heading: Code lives inside instances
sections.body:
Everything in a Roblox place is an **instance**: parts, folders, sounds, and scripts too. You see them all in the **Explorer** window, arranged in a tree. A script is just an instance whose job is to hold code, and the code is stored in its `Source` property.

That means where you put a script matters. The same code can run, do nothing, or run on the wrong computer, depending only on which folder it sits in. Learning the three kinds of script, and the right home for each, saves you hours of confusion later.

sections.heading: The three kinds of script
sections.body:
A `Script` runs on the **server**, the one computer that runs the real game and that every player connects to. Anything important, like money, damage or who wins, belongs here, because players can't tamper with the server.

A `LocalScript` runs on one player's **client**, their own device. It handles things only that player sees or does: their screen, their camera, their keyboard. Each player runs their own copy.

A `ModuleScript` doesn't run by itself at all. It holds code that other scripts borrow by calling `require` on it. You'll use these a lot from chapter 8 onwards, because they let many scripts share one piece of code.
bullets: `Script`: runs on the server. Lives in `ServerScriptService` (or the Workspace).
`LocalScript`: runs on each player's device. Lives in places like `StarterPlayerScripts` or `StarterGui`.
`ModuleScript`: runs only when another script requires it.

sections.heading: Why ServerScriptService
sections.body:
`ServerScriptService` is a folder only the server can see. Scripts inside it run when the game starts, and players never receive a copy of their code. That makes it the safest home for your game logic, and it's where nearly every test in this course lives.

A `Script` placed in `ReplicatedStorage` or `ServerStorage` won't run at all, because Roblox only starts scripts in certain places. If a script seems to do nothing, its location is the first thing to check.

sections.heading: Practising
sections.body:
Make a new **Baseplate** place in Studio and save it, for example as Luau Course. That's your playground for the lessons' Try it tasks, where you can watch code affect the world, so your pizza game never gets touched.

The chapter tests are different: you write them right here in the panel. Each test page has a small editor with one tab per script, a **Run** button that shows what your code prints, and a **Check my work** button that marks it straight away, with no Studio needed.

To run code in Studio, press **Play** or **Run** at the top. Run starts just the server, which is quicker when you only want to see what your scripts print.

key_points: Scripts are instances, and where you put them decides whether and where they run.
`Script` runs on the server, `LocalScript` on a player's device, `ModuleScript` only when required.
`ServerScriptService` is the safe home for server code, and the home of your course tests.
Lesson Try it tasks are for Studio. Chapter tests are written and checked in this panel.
mistakes: Putting a `Script` in `ReplicatedStorage` and wondering why it never runs.
Using a `LocalScript` for something important like money, which players could tamper with.
Practising inside your real game, where test scripts get mixed up with game scripts.
lessons.try_it: Set up your baseplate as described above. Add a Script inside `ServerScriptService` (not in your Course folder yet), press Run, and find the default "Hello world!" line in the Output window. Then move the script into `ReplicatedStorage`, run again, and notice that nothing prints.

quiz.question: You want to give a player 50 coins when they finish a delivery. Which kind of script should do it?
choices: A `LocalScript`, because it belongs to that player
A `ModuleScript` on its own, with nothing requiring it
Any of them, it makes no difference
quiz.explain: Money is important game state, so the server should decide it. A LocalScript runs on the player's device, which they control. A ModuleScript does nothing until something requires it.

quiz.question: A `Script` sits in `ReplicatedStorage`. What happens when you press Play?
quiz.explain: Roblox only starts Scripts in certain places, like ServerScriptService and the Workspace. In ReplicatedStorage it just sits there.

quiz.question: When does a `ModuleScript`'s code run?
choices: As soon as the game starts
quiz.explain: A ModuleScript is borrowed code. It runs when something calls require on it, and not before.

lessons.title: print, warn and comments
lessons.summary: Sending messages to the Output window, and leaving notes in your code that Luau ignores.

sections.heading: print
sections.body:
`print` writes a line to the **Output** window (open it from the View tab if you can't see it). It's how your code talks to you while you build, and it's the first tool you reach for when something isn't working.

You can give `print` several things at once, separated by commas. Roblox turns each one into text and joins them with a single space. Words in quotes are **strings** (text), while numbers and sums without quotes are worked out first, then printed.

Printing is also how professionals debug. When a script misbehaves, add a print before and after the part you suspect, run it, and see which lines appear. If the first prints and the second doesn't, the problem is between them. It feels basic, but it's quick, and it works everywhere.

example.caption: Several values in one print
example.explain: This prints `Lights on`, then `Lamps: 4 Broken: 1`, then `15`. The sum is worked out before it's printed.

sections.heading: warn
sections.body:
`warn` works exactly like `print`, but the line shows up in orange. Use it for things that aren't errors but deserve attention, like a missing part your script can work around.

The colour difference matters more than it sounds. In a busy Output window, orange lines jump out, so warnings get noticed while ordinary prints fade into the background.

There's also `error`, which you'll meet properly in chapter 8. It prints a red message and **stops** the script, the same way a real mistake does. That's different from warn, which only reports and lets the script carry on.

sections.heading: Comments
sections.body:
A **comment** is a note for humans that Luau skips completely. Two dashes start a comment that lasts until the end of the line. Two dashes followed by two square brackets start a comment that lasts until the closing brackets, which is handy for longer notes.

Good comments explain **why** code does something, because the code itself already shows what it does. A comment like "pause so the player notices the door" is useful. A comment like "wait 2 seconds" next to a two-second wait just repeats the code.

example.caption: Both kinds of comment
example.code:
-- A one-line comment
print("Ready") -- Comments can follow code too

--[[
	A longer comment
	can cover several lines
]]
example.explain: Only `Ready` prints. Everything after the dashes is ignored.

sections.heading: Turning code off with a comment
sections.body:
Putting `--` in front of a line "comments it out": the line stays in the script but no longer runs. It's a quick way to test whether a line is causing a problem without deleting it.

Studio can do this for you. Select some lines and press **Ctrl** with **/** to comment or uncomment them all at once.

sections.heading: Keep the Output tidy
sections.body:
When dozens of scripts all print, the Output window turns into noise and you stop noticing the line that matters. Print with a purpose, and say what each value is, like `print("Coins:", 25)` rather than a bare `25`. When you've fixed a problem, delete the prints you added to find it.

The Output window has a filter box at the top. Typing a word there hides every line that doesn't contain it, which is handy when one script's messages are buried among others.

key_points: `print` writes to the Output window, joining several values with spaces.
`warn` does the same in orange, for things that deserve attention.
`--` starts a one-line comment, and `--[[ ... ]]` a longer one.
Comments should explain why, not repeat what the code says.
mistakes: Forgetting the quotes around text, so Luau treats a word as a variable name and prints `nil`.
Leaving the Output window closed and thinking nothing printed.
Writing comments that only repeat the code.
lessons.try_it: In a Script on your baseplate, print your name, then print a sum like 12 times 4 without working it out yourself, then warn something. Comment out the warn line and run it again.

quiz.question: What does `print("Pizzas:", 3 + 2)` show in the Output window?
quiz.explain: The sum is worked out first, then print joins its values with a single space.

quiz.question: What's the difference between `print` and `warn`?
quiz.explain: They behave the same, but warn's line is orange so it stands out.

quiz.question: Which line runs?
quiz.explain: Both lines are comments, so Luau skips them entirely.

lessons.title: Reading error messages
lessons.summary: What an error tells you, how to find the line that caused it, and the errors you'll see most.

sections.heading: Errors are directions, not failures
sections.body:
When Luau hits something it can't do, it stops the script and prints an **error** in red. Beginners often panic and start changing random things, but an error message is the most useful thing Luau ever gives you. It says what went wrong and exactly where.

The skill is reading it calmly, word by word.

sections.heading: The shape of an error
sections.body:
An error usually looks like this: the script's full name, a colon, a line number, a colon, then the problem. For example, an error starting with `ServerScriptService.Course.Test01.Hello:4:` means line 4 of the script named `Hello` inside the `Test01` folder.

Click the red line in the Output window and Studio opens the script at that line. Then read the problem part. It names the operation that failed, like "attempt to perform arithmetic" or "attempt to call a nil value".

Below the error, a few lines starting with "Stack Begin" show which lines led there. You'll need that later, once your scripts call functions in other scripts.

If you see the same error many times, look at the first one. Later errors are often side effects of the first problem, and fixing it can make the rest disappear.

sections.heading: Syntax errors
sections.body:
A **syntax error** means Luau couldn't even understand the script, so none of it runs, not even the lines before the mistake. Studio underlines these in red while you type, which is your first warning.

Common causes are a missing closing quote or bracket, a missing `end`, or a misspelt keyword. The line number sometimes points just after the real mistake, because that's where Luau finally noticed something was off.

example.caption: A missing closing quote
example.explain: The first string never closes, so Luau reports a syntax error. Neither line runs.

sections.heading: Runtime errors
sections.body:
A **runtime error** happens while the script is running. Everything before the bad line has already run, then the script stops. Two you'll see constantly:

**attempt to perform arithmetic on a nil value** means you did maths with something that has no value, often a misspelt variable name. **attempt to call a nil value** means you tried to run something as a function that doesn't exist, often a misspelt function name, since Luau is case-sensitive and `Print` isn't `print`.

When you see `nil` in an error, think: what did I expect to have a value here, and why doesn't it?

sections.heading: A calm routine for any error
sections.body:
First, read the whole message out loud in your head, including the operation it names. Second, open the script at that line. Third, ask what value each name on that line has at that moment. Very often, one of them is `nil` because it was misspelt, never set, or set later in the script.

If you're stuck, add a print just before the failing line that shows the values involved. Seeing `nil` printed next to a name you were sure had a value usually solves the mystery in seconds. Debugging is a skill you build, and every error you read carefully makes the next one faster.

key_points: An error gives the script, the line number and the problem, in that order.
Clicking the error opens the script at the right line.
Syntax errors stop the whole script from running. Runtime errors stop it at the bad line.
`nil` in an error usually means a misspelt name or something that was never set.
mistakes: Changing code at random instead of reading the error.
Looking only at the reported line when a syntax error started on the line above.
Forgetting that names are case-sensitive, so `Print` and `print` are different.
lessons.try_it: Write a short script with three prints, then break it on purpose in different ways: remove a closing quote, misspell print as Print, and add a number to a name you never created. Read each error and predict which lines ran before it stopped.

quiz.question: An error begins `ServerScriptService.Course.Test01.Hello:7:`. What does the 7 mean?
choices: The problem is on line 7 of the script named Hello
There are 7 scripts in the folder
quiz.explain: The number after the script's name is the line where Luau hit the problem.

quiz.question: A script has a syntax error on line 5. What happens to lines 1 to 4?
choices: They run, then the script stops
Luau skips line 5 and runs everything else
quiz.explain: With a syntax error, Luau can't understand the script, so nothing in it runs.

quiz.question: What usually causes "attempt to call a nil value"?
choices: Calling a function name that doesn't exist, often a typo
quiz.explain: Luau looked up the name, found nothing (nil), and can't call nothing.

lessons.title: How code runs
lessons.summary: Statements, the top-to-bottom order Luau follows, and the small rules about spacing and case.

sections.heading: Top to bottom
sections.body:
A script is a list of **statements**, instructions like "print this". When the script starts, Luau runs them one at a time, from the top down, and each one finishes before the next begins. When it runs out of lines, the script is finished.

This sounds obvious, but it explains a lot of bugs. If line 3 uses something that line 8 sets up, line 3 runs first and finds nothing there yet. Order is part of what your code means.

Think of it like a recipe. You can't ice a cake before you bake it, and Luau won't skip ahead or go back unless you tell it to. In later chapters you'll learn the tools that change this flow: `if` statements that skip lines, loops that repeat them, and functions that run a block of code when you ask.

example.caption: Order decides the output
example.explain: These always print in exactly this order. Swap two lines and the joke falls apart.

sections.heading: Spacing and line breaks
sections.body:
Luau doesn't care about spaces, tabs or blank lines between statements. You could put two statements on one line, or spread one over several lines, and it would run the same. People use indentation and blank lines purely so code is easier to read, and Studio indents for you as you type.

That freedom isn't permission to be messy. You'll read your code far more often than you write it, so keep one statement per line and let indentation show the structure.

sections.heading: Case matters
sections.body:
Luau is **case-sensitive**: `print`, `Print` and `PRINT` are three different names, and only the first is the real print function. The same goes for every name you create yourself. This is one of the most common sources of `nil` errors, so when something "definitely exists" but Luau says it's nil, check the capital letters first.

When you create your own names later, pick one style and stick to it. Roblox's own API uses PascalCase for things like `ServerScriptService` and `WaitForChild`, and most scripters use camelCase for their own variables, like `deliveryCount`. Consistent naming means you rarely have to guess the capitals.

sections.heading: When scripts start
sections.body:
Every `Script` in `ServerScriptService` starts when the game starts, roughly at the same time, and you can't rely on which goes first. Each one runs on its own from its own top line. Later you'll learn ways to make scripts share code and wait for each other.

Every script also has an `Enabled` property. Untick it in the Properties window and the script won't run at all. That's how you'll stop old course tests from running while you work on new ones.

key_points: Luau runs statements one at a time, top to bottom.
Spacing and blank lines are for humans. Luau ignores them.
Untick a script's `Enabled` property to stop it running.
mistakes: Using something on one line that only gets set up on a later line.
Assuming one Script will run before another.
lessons.try_it: Make two Scripts in ServerScriptService that each print three numbered lines, press Run, and look at how their lines come out. Then untick one script's Enabled property and run again.

quiz.question: A script prints "A" on line 1 and "B" on line 2. What's guaranteed?
quiz.explain: Within one script, statements run in order from the top.

quiz.question: Two Scripts in ServerScriptService each print a line. Which prints first?
choices: You can't rely on the order
The one higher in the Explorer
The one with the shorter name
quiz.explain: Scripts start at roughly the same time, and their order isn't something to rely on.

quiz.question: How do you stop an old test script from running without deleting it?
choices: Add a blank line at the top
Move it to the bottom of the folder
quiz.explain: A script with Enabled turned off doesn't run, but keeps its code.
